title: Brazil separates credit advertising, debt-capacity disclosure and borrowing at Pix checkout
summary: The Banco Central do Brasil’s 5 November announcement described three approved rules targeting different stages of household borrowing. The intervention is especially relevant for analysing the transmission of high interest rates to vulnerable households. A change in new credit after implementation could reflect altered solicitation and disclosure as well as the level of rates. None of the three rules was reported as having taken effect on the November announcement date.

Resolution 602 addresses lender-initiated offers. Institutions must give customers a clear means of blocking active credit advertisements and offers. For customers identified as particularly financially vulnerable or at risk of excessive debt, an active offer needs prior, specific and unambiguous consent and must improve the customer’s position. The Bank gave renegotiations, transfers and moves to better products without fresh funds as examples. The customer can still approach a lender to obtain credit. The rule enters into force on 31 March 2027. Observed originations could therefore change differently for solicited loans, customer inquiries and restructurings.

Resolution 601 introduces an electronic consolidated debt dashboard. Before taking out a loan, the customer should be shown instalments, the share of monthly repayment capacity the transaction would absorb, and remaining capacity. The dashboard also provides debt details, cost simulations and automated warnings, including when debt service reaches 40% of monthly payment capacity. The 40% figure is an alert threshold. The release does not describe a binding maximum at which an application must be refused. Initially the dashboard covers obligations at the same institution. Later integration with the credit register and Open Finance should broaden coverage subject to applicable rules. Most provisions take effect on 1 July 2027.

Resolution 603 concerns lending offers during initiation of a Pix payment. Users must consent in advance and at least 24 hours must elapse between enabling the feature and the first offer. Institutions must provide information, including a credit simulator and access to contracted operations. The receiver continues to receive the full transfer immediately. These provisions also start on 1 July 2027. For merchant cash-flow analysis, the distinction between the payer’s financing decision and the recipient’s settlement is important. The rules could change the incidence of payers borrowing without changing how quickly a completed Pix reaches a merchant. No effects on volumes, defaults or spreads were reported.

questions.question: Does restricting lender-initiated marketing change expensive new borrowing among vulnerable households?
questions.detail: Compare solicited and customer-initiated applications around the March implementation, separating refinancings without new cash from loans that add principal. Measure fees, effective interest cost, subsequent arrears and borrower characteristics. A decline in the number of contracts would not necessarily signal less credit access if customers move into cheaper restructurings or initiate applications themselves.

questions.question: Does the dashboard’s 40% warning alter borrowing decisions or merely the amounts shown at a single bank?
questions.detail: Compare applications just above and below the warning threshold, checking how repayment capacity is defined and whether applicants or lenders can adjust the inputs. Distinguish the first phase, which sees only debts at the institution, from the later expansion. A fall in apparent debt burden can arise from switching providers even if the household’s total commitments are unchanged.

questions.question: Does the 24-hour interval reduce borrowing at Pix checkout without impeding payment completion?
questions.detail: Follow consent, activation, first offer, loan acceptance and payment completion as distinct events after July. Compare cohorts with similar purchases and prior access to credit, and check whether consumers shift to another credit channel. Receiver settlement time, the payer’s financing cost and merchant sales measure different outcomes. A payment count alone would not show whether the new design improved borrower outcomes.
